**Mumford-Tate group.** Having characterized the Deligne torus, or equivalently the action of the worldsheet R-symmetry, we next turn to the definition of the Mumford-Tate group. Consider the orbit \(h(\mathrm{U}(1))\) of this R-symmetry operator (6.9). At a generic point in moduli space this orbit will not be a \(\mathbb{Q}\)-algebraic<sup>26</sup> subgroup of the isometry group \(G\); one can see this for instance from the fact that generically most periods take transcendental values, i.e. the vectors spanning the spaces \(H^{p,q}\) have transcendental numbers as entries. However, at symmetric loci in moduli space there will be some algebraic relations among the periods, so the smallest \(\mathbb{Q}\)-algebraic subgroup that contains these orbits need not be the full isometry group \(G\) either. This is precisely where the Mumford-Tate group \(\mathrm{MT}(h)\) comes in, which is defined as the smallest \(\mathbb{Q}\)-algebraic subgroup of \(G\) containing \(h(\mathrm{U}(1))\), i.e. its \(\mathbb{Q}\)-algebraic closure.
